description: Procedure Deze inkoopprocedure betreft een open house-procedure. Alle aanbieders die voldoen aan de gestelde geschiktheidseisen, kwaliteitseisen en overige voorwaarden zoals opgenomen in de aanbestedingsstukken, komen in aanmerking voor het sluiten van een overeenkomst. Doel Het doel van deze open house-procedure is het contracteren van alle aanbieders die voldoen aan de gestelde eisen en voorwaarden, zodat een passende en voldoende dekkende infrastructuur beschikbaar is voor de uitvoering van specialistische ambulante behandeling binnen de regio West-Brabant Oost. Looptijd De overeenkomst heeft een looptijd van twee jaar en gaat in op 1 januari 2027. Na afloop van deze periode kan de overeenkomst tweemaal schriftelijk worden verlengd met telkens een periode van twaalf kalendermaanden. Mercell Deze inkoopprocedure wordt uitsluitend digitaal uitgevoerd via het platform Mercell (www.mercell.com). Via dit platform worden de aanbestedingsstukken beschikbaar gesteld, kunnen vragen worden gesteld en dienen aanmeldingen te worden ingediend. Nadere instructies over het gebruik van Mercell zijn opgenomen in de aanbestedingsstukken.

description: NHS South East London Integrated Care Board intends to commission a time-limited Primary Care Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) Hub for the London Borough of Bexley for winter 2026/27. The service will provide additional same-day urgent face-to-face appointment capacity for children and adults presenting with ARI-type symptoms, supporting general practice and the wider urgent and emergency care system during the period of increased winter demand. The service is expected to operate from a centrally located Bexley primary care location during core general practice hours, Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 18:30, and to be staffed by a GP and an Advanced Nurse Practitioner, supported by appropriate administrative capacity. Acute Respiratory Infection (ARI) hubs are a recognised NHS England model used across England to support the assessment and treatment of respiratory illness and to reduce pressure on emergency departments, urgent treatment centres and general practice. The proposed Bexley model reflects an established primary care-led approach that has operated within the borough over successive winter periods and is consistent with nationally recognised ARI hub delivery models. Key service objectives and outcomes • Provide additional same-day urgent primary care capacity for Bexley residents with ARI-type presentations during winter pressure. • Provide a clinically safe alternative pathway for people who can appropriately be managed in primary care, while maintaining clear escalation routes for patients requiring urgent or emergency treatment. • Support timely access for adults and children referred by Bexley general practice and NHS 111. • Support resilience across Bexley general practice and the wider urgent and emergency care system. • Deliver equitable access, with operational monitoring to identify and respond to variation in referral, utilisation and outcomes across patient groups and localities. • Maintain effective integration with general practice, NHS 111, urgent treatment and secondary care pathways. buyer: NHS North East London Integrated Care Board
title: High Intensity User (HIU) Programme - Outcomes Partnership (Market Engagement)
description: NHS North East London Integrated Care Board (NEL ICB) is exploring the market ahead of seeking to commission an ICB-wide High Intensity User (HIU) Outcomes Partnership. The provider must have proven experience in delivering preventative health Social Outcomes Partnerships, be willing to undertake co-design with NEL ICB at risk, and have access to at least £1.0m of approved social investment risk capital available for drawdown upon contract award. Health and care systems face a growing, structural challenge: a small number of people experiencing the deepest deprivation and complexity account for a disproportionate share of urgent and emergency care demand. This is not a marginal issue; it is a material driver of pressure, cost and inequality across the NHS. High Intensity Use is predictable, persistent, and concentrated. It is driven by unmet social need, trauma, poor access to community-based support and fragmented systems. Left unaddressed, it results in repeated crisis presentations, poor outcomes for individuals and escalating system cost. High Intensity Use of urgent and emergency care represents a significant and growing challenge across UK health systems. National evaluation evidence shows that fewer than one per cent of people account for approximately: • 16% of A&E attendances. • 29% of ambulance arrivals. • 26% of emergency admissions. This activity is estimated to cost the NHS at least £2.5 billion per year. Individuals with repeated attendances are highly likely to continue using emergency care unless targeted intervention occurs. By a person's eighth emergency attendance within a year, there is a greater than 50% likelihood that they will continue to attend frequently for at least two years, rising to over 80% by the fifteenth attendance. This creates a clearly identifiable cohort for targeted preventative intervention. There are proven delivery models addressing these challenges, with a track record of reducing secondary care usage for high intensity users. However, despite the potential to improve outcomes for these individuals and reduce demand on the system, funding for these interventions has traditionally been both small compared to the need, and short-term. An outcomes approach offers a potential solution to this. Outcomes partnerships are services where 100% of the funding is linked to evidenced outcomes achieved by individuals on the Programme. They add value in issue areas which require a change in policy focus (i.e., from sickness to prevention) through creating an environment to test ideas, build and develop new services, or continue to improve existing ones. The work is proposed to consist of two phases: 1. A Co-design phase working with NEL to develop the delivery model and outcomes framework, and; 2. the delivery of the intervention. The co-design phase will include analysis of existing services, gaps in provisions, and local priorities to identify the target cohort, geography, and total contract value for the service. This would be followed by co-design of the delivery model, facilitating input from all key stakeholders (including Hospital MDT leads and patients), and joint development of an outcomes framework. A key feature of an outcomes partnership is the flexibility of the delivery model, which can be improved over time as the Programme learns what works. The typical duration of support is expected to be between 9 to 12 weeks, but this will vary depending on the cohort to ensure sustained improvement and positive health outcomes. The outcomes the service would be targeting include: • Improved wellbeing and patient activation. • Improvement in wider social determinants of health including housing, financial situation, and loneliness. • Reduce use of secondary care services including; A&E attendances, Emergency admissions, and Ambulance conveyances.

title: 715864481 - Preliminary Market Engagement RFI Debrief – LIOS IROC/OP&S
description: The Authority recently carried out a Pre Market Engagement (PME) exercise in support of the Integrated Readiness Output Contract (IROC) and Other Platforms and Services (OP&S) elements of the wider Land Integrated Operating Services (LIOS) programme. The Authority can now update industry partners on common themes within the PME responses received and key updates. LIOS is a once in a generation opportunity to begin the transformation of Land vehicle support from 2026, with a full LIOS enterprise in place from 2030) and, in doing so, bring MOD and Industry closer to delivering Defence’s intent in accordance with the Land Industrial Strategy. The vision for LIOS is to deliver long-term, output-focussed equipment support solutions that proactively and intelligently manage in-scope capabilities through-life in accordance with capability management plans. LIOS will deliver sustainable enterprise efficiencies to optimise support and capabilities through-life, combining upkeep, update, and upgrade services. IROC, including but not limited to provision of the services currently delivered via the extant Service Provision and Transformation Contract (SPTC), covers a wide range of in-service land equipment and is intended to be a pan Integrated Operating Service (IOS) service provider incentivised to reduce duplication of work, maximise pan-Defence Lines of Development (DLOD) non-Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) efficiencies and leverage economies of scale. OP&S including but not limited to provision of post-design services (PDS) via contracts such as PMETS and other support services for in-scope platforms not included within platform IOS contracts from April 2030 and will provide IOS support for those platforms that continue beyond 2030 but do not have a planned programme of Upgrades and Update. IROC and OP&S are initially being managed as one over-arching programme until the procurement strategy is matured however there may be two or more procurements. The role and full scope of the services will be developed and matured prior to formal procurement activity commencing.
